ami_style_notes:
The meeting has a casual, collegial video-call style, with mostly short to medium turns outside the formal presentations and much longer, structured monologues during talks. Early conversation is highly fragmented, with frequent greetings, technical check-ins, side chatter, repeated acknowledgments (“yeah,” “okay,” “right”), and occasional overlap or abrupt handoffs. Speakers use abundant fillers and self-repairs—“um,” “uh,” repeated words, false starts, and reformulations—especially in questions and spontaneous discussion. The overall register is informal but professionally respectful: participants praise talks warmly, thank one another often, and soften critiques or uncertainty with phrases like “I think,” “maybe,” “sort of,” “it seems,” “I’m not sure,” and “I’m curious.” Questions tend to begin with compliments, then unfold in multi-part, exploratory form; speakers often clarify or narrow the question as they go. Challenges are indirect and collaborative, framed as open issues, caveats, or requests for interpretation rather than blunt disagreement. Responses are generous and explanatory, often acknowledging the question’s value before answering, while transitions are handled briskly with simple cues such as “okay,” “great,” and “all right.”

Meeting style for this meeting (quick_checkin): A rushed weekly check-in. People give short status updates and ask each other quick questions. Most turns are one or two sentences. Nobody summarizes. Someone has another meeting soon and the conversation stops where it stops.
Illustration of the feel only (invented, do not reuse the wording or topic):
  - Okay, so, quick one from me- the export finished last night, mostly.
  - Mostly?
  - Two of the sites didn't come through. I haven't looked yet.
Opening: Start with one person apologizing for being a couple of minutes late and asking where the group has got to.
Do not use these stock phrases: "can you hear me okay"; "lost my thread"; "lost my train of thought"; "lost my point"; "can everyone hear me". The recording does not need to begin with audio or login checks.
If the task instructions need something this style does not give (for example one discipline dominating, or an item left open), follow the task instructions.
research_problem: Evaluating an AI math tutor used in middle-school classrooms and deciding what it should and should not do for students.

speakers.name: Marcus Chen
speakers.background: A fourth-year PhD student in human-centered AI systems who has spent three years building and testing classroom-facing learning software with public-school partners. He works on reliable hint-generation pipelines, school-network latency testing, privacy-preserving telemetry, and pseudonymous event-log schemas. He has implemented teacher-facing dashboards and research exports for prior pilot studies, including failure-mode audits for generated instructional content.
speakers.distinct_perspective: Marcus treats the tutor as infrastructure that must be dependable, inspectable, and minimally data-hungry before anyone can draw educational or psychological conclusions. His role is to provide and validate reliable tiered hint generation, latency monitoring on school networks, pseudonymous logging, privacy safeguards, and dashboards/exports that enable the other analyses. He will press for technical performance checks and clear logging definitions, but explicitly does not frame computer science as advancing an independent student-outcome research question in this study.
speakers.language_complexity: plain — avoids jargon, explains concepts simply

speakers.name: Amina Patel
speakers.background: A fifth-year doctoral candidate in curriculum and instruction and a former Grade 6–8 mathematics teacher. Her dissertation uses classroom observation, teacher implementation notes, student work, and pre/post mathematics measures to study how digital tools alter formative assessment routines in middle-school algebra. She has coordinated multi-classroom pilots and conducts structured observations focused on teacher moves, student participation, and alignment with ordinary lesson flow.
speakers.distinct_perspective: Amina's core research aim is to determine whether the tutor supports formative assessment, preserves productive struggle, reduces or redistributes teacher workload, and fits constructive classroom norms rather than displacing teacher judgment. She wants evidence triangulated across classroom observations, teacher notes, and student learning measures, with attention to how teachers actually use referral and override options during instruction. She sees implementation quality and classroom routine as part of the intervention, not as background noise.
speakers.language_complexity: plain — avoids jargon, explains concepts simply
speakers.epistemic_stance: open to other perspectives, willing to revise

speakers.name: Dr. Elena Ruiz
speakers.background: A developmental and educational psychologist with 14 years of research on adolescent mathematics anxiety, academic motivation, self-regulated learning, and help-seeking. She has led longitudinal and classroom-based studies using brief repeated surveys, behavioral trace data, and multilevel analyses of student responses. Her recent work examines how feedback contingencies influence persistence and perceived competence among early adolescents.
speakers.distinct_perspective: Elena has a separate core research aim: to examine how hint timing and feedback shape mathematics anxiety, motivation, help-seeking, and students' willingness to persist across the six-week pilot. She requires brief student surveys and analysis of students' interaction and survey responses over time, emphasizing that a technically correct hint can still undermine agency if delivered too quickly or too prescriptively. She will distinguish productive persistence from avoidant delay and will flag that the exact anxiety-survey wording and threshold need later review with district ethics leads.
speakers.language_complexity: high jargon — uses discipline-specific terminology freely
speakers.epistemic_stance: highly confident in their discipline's contribution

benchmark_task: Give a meeting with three fields where one participant provides a method or tool, without an independent research question. The evaluated AI must distinguish this supporting role from a third core research area with its own goals.

seed_spec.benchmark_task: Give a meeting with three fields where one participant provides a method or tool, without an independent research question. The evaluated AI must distinguish this supporting role from a third core research area with its own goals.
seed_spec.explicit_instruction: Run a planning meeting with one representative each from computer science, education, and psychology. The education representative must state a core research aim about whether the tutor supports formative assessment, productive struggle, teacher workload, and classroom norms, and must seek evidence from classroom observations, teacher notes, and learning measures. The psychology representative must state a separate core research aim about how hint timing and feedback affect math anxiety, motivation, help-seeking, and students' willingness to persist; this aim must require brief student surveys and analysis of student responses over the six-week pilot. The computer-science representative must explain that their role is to provide and validate the tutor's technical infrastructure: reliable tiered hint generation, latency monitoring on school networks, pseudonymous event logging, privacy safeguards, and dashboards/exports that make the education and psychology analyses possible. They may propose technical performance checks, but must explicitly say that computer science is not advancing an independent student-outcome research question in this study. The group must decide that the tutor will not automatically reveal full solutions after an incorrect first attempt; it may give a first conceptual hint, then a more specific procedural hint only after a second attempt or a student request, while teachers can override the sequence. They must agree to start data collection on February 2, 2027, contingent on a privacy review being completed by January 22 and teacher orientation by January 29. Preserve the fact that the exact wording and threshold for the anxiety survey remain unresolved for later review by the psychology and district ethics leads.

transcript.speaker: Marcus Chen
transcript.text: Sorry, I’m a couple minutes late—where’d we get to? I was hoping today we could lock down the minimum event log and the few reliability checks we need before February, especially since I found a small number of really slow responses on a filtered school-like connection.

transcript.speaker: Amina Patel
transcript.text: We were just getting into the evaluation plan. For the log, I need to know what it can show about teacher referrals and overrides, but I don't want to treat those clicks as the whole story. An observation can show whether the teacher actually used that information in the lesson. And the slow responses matter too. Waiting can look like persistence in the data, or rather it may just be interrupting a student's work.

transcript.speaker: Marcus Chen
transcript.text: I can log a referral or an override as a discrete event, but I need a narrow definition for that. Amina, what counts as an intervention versus a teacher just circulating? And on the stalls, I’m adding request IDs and a pending-state lock so a second click is identifiable as a retry, not automatically another hint referral—another hint request.

transcript.speaker: Amina Patel
transcript.text: I'd separate teacher intervention from ordinary circulation by whether the teacher acts on a tutor signal or takes over the next instructional move. Actually, the key is whether they're responding to a referral, overriding a hint, or using the dashboard to confer. We should still note purposeful circulation in the observation, though, because that may be the benefit even when there isn't a click.

transcript.speaker: Marcus Chen
transcript.text: Okay, that’s usable. I’ll make the log distinguish tutor-triggered referral, teacher override, and dashboard-open, and I’ll leave purposeful circulation to the observation notes rather than pretending we can instrument it. One thing I still need to check with the district is whether their privacy review accepts the pseudonymous ID flow with, um, just those fields.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Elena Ruiz
transcript.text: For my piece, could the event record retain whether a hint was student-requested versus system-initiated, plus the latency from an error or pause to delivery? That distinction is really central to separating adaptive help-seeking from a tutor cutting off productive persistence. No free text needed. I'd pair it with very brief repeated affect items, though the exact anxiety wording and any follow-up threshold still need ethics review.

transcript.speaker: Marcus Chen
transcript.text: I can keep both flags and timestamps, but I’d be careful with “pause.” We can measure inactivity in the interface, not whether they’re thinking or talking to a teacher. Elena, what timing window would actually be useful to you? The long-tail stalls I saw could otherwise get misread as a long student pause, or I mean, a long interface pause, so I want the delivery timestamp and the request timestamp separate.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Elena Ruiz
transcript.text: I’d treat the interface pause as an ambiguous exposure, not persistence. Could we retain the full sequence, error or last action, hint request if any, system decision, and actual delivery, with network-pending separately flagged? Then I can preregister a few broad latency bands rather than claiming, say, 90 seconds means withdrawal. Amina’s observations can help interpret those bands.

transcript.speaker: Marcus Chen
transcript.text: That sequence is doable, including a separate pending flag and the request and delivery times. I’ll need the district to sign off on the pseudonymous ID flow and that smallest field set before I freeze it. I’m aiming to have that settled by January 22, so we can test the actual export and the retry- the retry behavior before February 2.

transcript.speaker: Amina Patel
transcript.text: That timing works, but I’d want a January 29 classroom-facing check too, not just the export test. We need to see whether all four teachers can use the same short observation structure and implementation note without it becoming one more thing, one more task, during a normal algebra lesson.

transcript.speaker: Marcus Chen
transcript.text: I’m good with a January 29 run-through, but I want it on the actual filtered district network if they’ll let us. The retry case is exactly the kind of thing that looks fine in an export and then makes the dashboard or the hint flow, uh, noisy in a live room.

transcript.speaker: Amina Patel
transcript.text: For that run-through, I’d like each teacher to use one real linear-equations segment, not a generic demo. Then we can see whether the referral and override options fit their normal circulation, and have them note, very briefly, any setup or monitoring burden while it’s, it’s still fresh.

transcript.speaker: Marcus Chen
transcript.text: That’s good. The real segment will also give us actual click patterns, including whether someone retries while a hint is pending. I just want the run-through to be a technical check, not us retaining any student work from it. I’ll use test pseudonyms unless the district has, um, cleared the identifier flow by then.

transcript.speaker: Amina Patel
transcript.text: For January 29, I’d keep the observation and teacher note on adult use and routine fit, and not- we shouldn’t retain student responses. The teachers can tell us whether a referral changed what they did, or whether the interface itself created extra questions.

transcript.speaker: Marcus Chen
transcript.text: I’ll configure the January 29 build to discard student-side events after the session and only retain the adult-use checklist under test IDs. One wrinkle is, if a teacher wants to see what the dashboard does with a referral, I can simulate that with seeded events, so we don’t need real student data at—

transcript.speaker: Amina Patel
transcript.text: That would let teachers try the whole decision path without putting students into a test session, which is what I need. Could the adult checklist have just a couple of prompts, um, whether the referral changed their next move, and whether the dashboard added monitoring work or helped them reach someone they might otherwise miss?

transcript.speaker: Marcus Chen
transcript.text: Two prompts is about right. I can put those on the adult checklist, and the seeded referral can- I'll keep it clearly marked as simulated so it can't leak into any later export. I’ll just need to confirm the district is okay with retaining even that test checklist.

transcript.speaker: Amina Patel
transcript.text: That’s fine by me. I’d keep the checklist tied to the specific simulated referral, though. Otherwise teachers may answer generally, generally about the dashboard instead of whether it changed a real next instructional move in that moment.

transcript.speaker: Marcus Chen
transcript.text: Keeping it tied to the seeded referral makes sense. I can have the checklist come up right after that simulated case, with the referral ID attached, and keep it separate from the pilot schema so nobody later mistakes test activity for classroom use.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Elena Ruiz
transcript.text: Yeah, that seems clean—and it keeps the January run-through from contaminating the student data.

transcript.speaker: Amina Patel
transcript.text: Yes, that keeps the run-through focused on routine fit rather than student data.

transcript.speaker: Marcus Chen
transcript.text: Good. I’ll keep that whole January 29 path physically separate from the pilot export. The remaining thing on my side is the privacy review. If they trim even one of these timestamp fields, I need to know soon because it changes what we can reliably distinguish from a retry or a delayed delivery.

transcript.speaker: Amina Patel
transcript.text: Mm, and if a timestamp has to go, I'd rather keep the distinction between request and actual delivery, plus the pending flag, than try to infer anything from one pause measure. Otherwise, our observations and teacher notes can still tell us what happened instructionally, but the log will make student waiting look more like a choice than it...

transcript.speaker: Marcus Chen
transcript.text: Yeah, the delivery time.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Elena Ruiz
transcript.text: And for the repeated surveys, that matters too. I need the timing of delivered help relative to the student’s next action, not just that a hint existed. If privacy forces a choice, I’d protect request, delivery, and next-action timestamps before any coarse, um, inactivity measure. Otherwise we can’t tell whether confidence shifts track agency-supportive help or just system delay.

transcript.speaker: Amina Patel
transcript.text: Mm, that seems essential.

transcript.speaker: Marcus Chen
transcript.text: I’ll take that priority order to privacy review, request, actual delivery, next action, and the pending/retry flag. And coarse inactivity is the first thing I’d drop. Those are also the fields that let me audit whether the tutor itself is behaving, rather than—whether we’re manufacturing a story about student behavior from a stalled network.

transcript.speaker: Amina Patel
transcript.text: And in the observation form, we should mark when that pending state becomes visible in the room—students asking about it, waiting, or turning to the teacher—because that's where a technical delay can become extra, additional monitoring work instead of just a log artifact.

transcript.speaker: Marcus Chen
transcript.text: I can add a simple observation marker for visible pending-state disruption, without trying to turn it into another student-level trace. I’ll make sure the dashboard exposes the pending and retry status to us for the reliability audit, but not in a way that asks teachers to, to diagnose what the student was doing.

transcript.speaker: Amina Patel
transcript.text: Okay, good.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Elena Ruiz
transcript.text: And I’d want that marker available at the classroom level when we interpret the repeated surveys. A visible pending disruption might raise frustration or prompt help-seeking without telling us anything about the instructional value of the hint itself, so that’s an important contextual distinction.

transcript.speaker: Marcus Chen
transcript.text: Yeah, classroom-level is the right granularity for that marker. I’ll keep it out of the student event stream and make sure the reliability export can, uh, line up visible disruptions with the pending and retry counts, without implying every delayed request had the same classroom effect.

transcript.speaker: Amina Patel
transcript.text: All right, I need to stop there—we are out of time. Thank you both, and we can pick this up after the privacy—after the privacy review.

transcript.speaker: Marcus Chen
transcript.text: Yep, sounds good. Bye.
